rv.q: McPherson’s book is a haunting slice of Depression-era Americana that draws not only on Dylan’s songbook but finds inspiration in the sad, vivid pages of authors like John Steinbeck and other chroniclers of the wrenching upheaval of the 1930s in the US.
Girl From the North Country is a kind of musical palimpsest, a prism through which to view a familiar body of work from an unusual but enchanting perspective.

It's an inventive piece of writing that, in the end, proves frustratingly diffuse; there's a nagging suspicion that McPherson — who also directs — never quite has control over his sprawling cast of characters.
Quite simply, Girl From the North Country continues its legacy as an unforgettable piece of theatre.
With a tender dialogue between acting and singing, McPherson moulds a story for the stage that both touches the heart and pleases the ears.

cn.t: McPherson's acclaimed musical returns to the West End with a new cast, weaving Dylan's songs into a haunting Depression-era tale. Critics praise the tender blend of acting and singing, with electric energy bringing the poignant story to life.
